You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content: "38 :     public NotPositiveDefiniteMatrixException() {\n39 :         super(\"not positive definite matrix\");\n40 :     }"

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The test case `testNotPositiveDefinite` is designed to check if the `CholeskyDecompositionImpl` correctly throws a `NotPositiveDefiniteMatrixException` when provided a matrix that is not symmetric positive definite. The constructor of `CholeskyDecompositionImpl` (lines 93-151) enforces validation: it first ensures the matrix is square, then checks each diagonal element against an absolute positivity threshold throwing `NotPositiveDefiniteMatrixException` if any diagonal element is below this threshold (line 114-115). It also checks for symmetry by comparing off-diagonal elements within a relative threshold and throws `NotSymmetricMatrixException` if the matrix is not symmetric (lines 124-125). This explains the intent of the test.

The test input matrix used in the failing test (lines 71-77) is a 5x5 matrix which is expected to be not positive definite, so the exception should be thrown. However, given the exception is not triggered (test fails), it implies the matrix passes the positivity check (diagonal elements >= threshold) and symmetry checks causing the constructor to complete successfully and further lines in the test (like printing the multiplication of getL() and getLT()) to execute.

This suggests a failure in detecting non-positive definiteness of the input matrix during construction. Possible issues include the threshold values being too lax (default thresholds might be too permissive) or the matrix input accidentally meeting conditions checked by the code. Since the test expects the `NotPositiveDefiniteMatrixException` but none is thrown, the problem lies in the fault detection logic in the constructor of `CholeskyDecompositionImpl` specifically around lines 114-115 and how thresholds are applied or matrix data is interpreted.

No issues are seen in `getL()` or `getLT()` which only return cached or transposed matrix components. The exception class itself is straightforward.

In summary, the root cause is the constructor's failure to identify the matrix as not positive definite due to either incorrect threshold usage or matrix data handling in the validation loop prior to decomposition. This results in the test unexpectedly passing without throwing the expected exception.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
